Chapter 2: Theological Awakening—Wrestling with Faith and the Modern World
University life, as you probably know, has a way of opening doors you didn’t even realize were there. For our young theologian, stepping onto campus was like stepping into a whole new world. Suddenly, he’s surrounded by ideas that spark his curiosity—but also leave him feeling a bit unsettled. Professors aren’t just teaching facts; they’re challenging what he thought he knew about the Bible, about the church, and about what it means to have faith in a world that’s changing faster than ever.
Some of his classmates seem happy to treat theology like it’s just another subject to study, but for him? It’s personal. It’s a matter of life and death. So he spends late nights in the library, digging deep into ancient texts and modern commentaries, searching for answers to questions that have been haunting him since he was a kid. What does it really mean to follow Christ when the world around you seems indifferent—or even hostile—to faith? Is being a Christian just about believing certain things, or is it about living those beliefs, even when it costs you something?
Travel soon becomes an essential part of his journey. Imagine him in Rome, standing in awe beneath towering cathedrals, taking in the beauty of worship that crosses every language and border. For the first time, he sees the global church—a community that’s so much bigger than any one place or culture. It’s a powerful reminder: the church isn’t just a local club. It’s a living, breathing community, called to point beyond itself to something greater.
But here’s something he can’t ignore—he also sees the church’s flaws. He notices how easily faith can get tangled up with power, and how quickly religious institutions can drift away from their true mission. It bothers him, but instead of turning away, it strengthens his resolve. If the church is really going to matter, it has to be willing to stand apart, to speak truth—even when it means standing alone.
Then there’s his time in America, especially in Harlem. There, he finds a community of believers whose faith has been shaped by suffering and injustice. The music, the preaching, and the hope that pulses through every gathering—it all leaves a mark on him. He comes to see that faith isn’t just about what you believe; it’s about what you do. It’s about standing with those who’ve been pushed aside, and turning beliefs into action.
Returning to Germany, he begins to put these lessons into words. He writes, he teaches, and he challenges others to see that true faith is never just comfortable or complacent. It asks something of us. It calls us to risk, to sacrifice, and to live for something bigger than ourselves.
Of course, not everyone’s ready for that message. Some of his colleagues roll their eyes, calling him idealistic—or even naïve. But he can’t let go of the conviction that the church has to be more than just a mirror of the world’s values. It needs to be a prophetic voice, calling people to a higher standard.
And as political tensions in Germany start to rise, these questions become even more urgent. A dangerous new ideology is taking shape, threatening to change the very fabric of the nation. The church has a choice: will it go along, or will it stand up and resist? For our young theologian, the answer is clear. But he knows that the road ahead is going to be anything but easy.
